title: Virtual reality and augmented reality-supported K-12 STEM learning: trends, advantages and challenges
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing body of research on how virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are being used in K-12 STEM education, with the goal of identifying publication trends, common design choices, benefits, and implementation challenges. The authors note a gap in comprehensive synthesis across STEM subjects and across both immersive and non-immersive VR/AR technologies, especially in the more recent literature from 2018–2022.

To answer this question, the authors conducted a PRISMA-based systematic review of 117 empirical studies published between 2010 and 2022 and indexed in Web of Science. They coded studies by subject area, device type, participant grade band, research method, sample size, and learning strategy. The review includes K-12 students across elementary, middle, and high school levels, with studies drawn primarily from science education, but also mathematics and integrated STEM learning.

The review concludes that VR/AR-supported K-12 STEM research has grown rapidly, with the strongest evidence base in science and much less attention to technology and engineering. Non-immersive tools, especially smartphone/tablet-based AR and desktop VR, were more common than immersive devices. Reported benefits include improved achievement, motivation, self-efficacy, attention, satisfaction, and engagement, while challenges include distraction, operational difficulty, teacher classroom-management issues, school costs, infrastructure limits, and privacy concerns. The authors argue that future work should focus more on technology and engineering learning, immersive devices, senior high school settings, and 21st-century skills.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of empirical studies, but it does not synthesize a single pooled effect size and relies on heterogeneous primary studies with varying designs. The evidence is strong as a descriptive review, but it is not a meta-analysis or a single well-controlled causal study.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports many positive findings, including multiple studies on achievement, motivation, and engagement, with at least one large effect reported (d=1.28 for attention). However, the evidence is heterogeneous and mixed across outcomes and comparators, so the overall impact is modest rather than definitively large.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of VR and AR-supported K-12 STEM learning, including immersive virtual environments, augmented science labs, and game-based learning activities used to teach science, mathematics, and integrated STEM concepts.

finding.finding_summary: Across 117 empirical studies, the review reports that VR/AR was associated with improved STEM learning outcomes, especially in science contexts, but effects were not uniformly positive. The paper summarizes that 60 studies found improved academic achievement, with examples such as an AR-supported laboratory study where students scored significantly higher than those in a traditional classroom, while some comparisons showed no significant difference versus other digital tools like video.
finding.measure: Academic achievement, learning performance, learning outcomes, test scores in VR/AR-supported STEM learning
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; individual primary studies varied

finding.finding_summary: The review found consistent positive effects on motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, satisfaction, attention, and engagement in K-12 STEM learning with VR/AR. It reports 27 studies showing improved motivation, 14 on self-efficacy, 13 on positive attitudes, 11 on satisfaction, and 12 on attention/concentration, indicating strong affective and engagement benefits.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, satisfaction, attention, engagement/participation, cognitive load-related affective measures
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; counts reported for sub-outcomes
finding.effect_size: d=1.28 (attention, one cited study); otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that VR/AR can support higher-order outcomes such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, analytical ability, metacognitive awareness, and cooperation. These benefits were less frequently studied than achievement and motivation, but the paper identifies 11 studies on cognitive abilities and 3 studies on cooperative ability as positive examples.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving skills, analytical ability, metacognitive awareness, leadership/decision-making/trust-building in collaboration
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; sub-outcome counts reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports some evidence that VR/AR can improve learning efficiency and effectiveness, but also notes that these technologies can introduce time costs and operational burdens. One cited study found students in virtual environments reached objectives faster, while other studies reported novelty-related time consumption, device-operation problems, and lower efficiency in some settings.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency, learning effectiveness, operational ease, task completion time
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; sub-outcome counts reported
